This guide is for AI coding agents working in the Svelte monorepo.

**Important:** Read and follow [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](./CONTRIBUTING.md) as well - it contains essential information about testing, code structure, and contribution guidelines that applies here.

When submitting a PR, you **MUST** read [`PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`](./.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md) and fill it out correctly. **DO NOT** submit a PR without running the full test suite.

## Quick Reference

If asked to do a performance investigation, use the `performance-investigation` skill.

# Contributing to Svelte

Svelte is a new way to build web applications. It's a compiler that takes your declarative components and converts them into efficient JavaScript that surgically updates the DOM.

The [Open Source Guides](https://opensource.guide/) website has a collection of resources for individuals, communities, and companies. These resources help people who want to learn how to run and contribute to open source projects. Contributors and people new to open source alike will find the following guides especially useful:

- [How to Contribute to Open Source](https://opensource.guide/how-to-contribute/)
- [Building Welcoming Communities](https://opensource.guide/building-community/)

## Get involved

There are many ways to contribute to Svelte, and many of them do not involve writing any code. Here are a few ideas to get started:

- Simply start using Svelte. Go through the [Getting Started](https://svelte.dev/docs#getting-started) guide. Does everything work as expected? If not, we're always looking for improvements. Let us know by [opening an issue](#reporting-new-issues).
- Look through the [open issues](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues). A good starting point would be issues tagged [good first issue](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22). Provide workarounds, ask for clarification, or suggest labels. Help [triage issues](#triaging-issues-and-pull-requests).
- If you find an issue you would like to fix, [open a pull request](#pull-requests).
- Read through our [tutorials](https://svelte.dev/tutorial). If you find anything that is confusing or can be improved, you can make edits by clicking "Edit this page" at the bottom left of the tutorial page.
- Take a look at the [features requested](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/labels/feature%20request) by others in the community and consider opening a pull request if you see something you want to work on.

Contributions are very welcome. If you think you need help planning your contribution, please ping us on Discord at [svelte.dev/chat](https://svelte.dev/chat) and let us know you are looking for a bit of help.

### Triaging issues and pull requests

One great way you can contribute to the project without writing any code is to help triage issues and pull requests as they come in.

- Ask for more information if you believe the issue does not provide all the details required to solve it.
- Flag issues that are stale or that should be closed.
- Ask for test plans and review code.

## Our process

### RFCs

If you'd like to propose an implementation for a large new feature or change then please [create an RFC](https://github.com/sveltejs/rfcs) to discuss it up front.

### Roadmap

When deciding where to contribute, you may wish to take a look at [our roadmap](https://svelte.dev/roadmap). The Svelte team generally works on a single major effort at a time. This has a couple benefits for us as maintainers. First, it allows us to focus and make noticeable progress in an area being proactive rather than reactive. Secondly, it allows us to handle related issues and PRs together. By batching issues and PRs together we’re able to ensure implementations and fixes holistically address the set of problems and use cases encountered by our users.

### Maintainer meetings

The maintainers meet on the final Saturday of each month. While these meetings are not open publicly, we will report back by leaving a comment on each issue discussed. We will generally discuss items aligning with our roadmap, but major PRs needing discussion amongst the maintainers can be added to the agenda for the monthly maintainer’s meeting. However, we typically are only able to get to a couple of items that are not aligned with our current priority.

### Prioritization

We do our best to review PRs and RFCs as they are sent, but it is difficult to keep up. We welcome help in reviewing PRs, RFCs, and issues. If an item aligns with the current priority on our [roadmap](https://svelte.dev/roadmap), it is more likely to be reviewed quickly. PRs to the most important and active repositories get reviewed more quickly while PRs to smaller inactive repos may sit for a bit before we periodically come by and review the pending PRs in a batch.

## Bugs

We use [GitHub issues](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues) for our public bugs. If you would like to report a problem, take a look around and see if someone already opened an issue about it. If you are certain this is a new unreported bug, you can submit a [bug report](#reporting-new-issues).

If you have questions about using Svelte, contact us on Discord at [svelte.dev/chat](https://svelte.dev/chat), and we will do our best to answer your questions.

If you see anything you'd like to be implemented, create a [feature request issue](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/new?template=feature_request.yml).

### Reporting new issues

When [opening a new issue](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/new/choose), always make sure to fill out the issue template. **This step is very important!** Not doing so may result in your issue not being managed in a timely fashion. Don't take this personally if this happens, and feel free to open a new issue once you've gathered all the information required by the template.

- **One issue, one bug:** Please report a single bug per issue.
- **Provide reproduction steps:** List all the steps necessary to reproduce the issue. The person reading your bug report should be able to follow these steps to reproduce your issue with minimal effort. If possible, use the [REPL](https://svelte.dev/repl) to create your reproduction.

## Pull requests

### Proposing a change

If you would like to request a new feature or enhancement but are not yet thinking about opening a pull request, you can also file an issue with [feature template](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/new?template=feature_request.yml).

If you're only fixing a bug, it's fine to submit a pull request right away, but we still recommend that you file an issue detailing what you're fixing. This is helpful in case we don't accept that specific fix but want to keep track of the issue.

Small pull requests are much easier to review and more likely to get merged.

### Installation

Ensure you have [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/installation) installed. After cloning the repository, run `pnpm install`.

### Developing

To build the UMD version of `svelte/compiler` (this is only necessary for CommonJS consumers, or in-browser use), run `pnpm build` inside `packages/svelte`. To rebuild whenever source files change, run `pnpm dev`.

### Creating a branch

Fork [the repository](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte) and create your branch from `main`. If you've never sent a GitHub pull request before, you can learn how from [this free video series](https://egghead.io/courses/how-to-contribute-to-an-open-source-project-on-github).

### Testing

A good test plan has the exact commands you ran and their output, provides screenshots or videos if the pull request changes UI.

- If you've changed APIs, update the documentation.

#### Writing tests

All tests are located in the `/tests` folder.

Test samples are kept in `/tests/xxx/samples` folders.

title: Overview
---

Svelte is a framework for building user interfaces on the web. It uses a compiler to turn declarative components written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript...

```svelte
<!--- file: App.svelte --->
<script>
	function greet() {
		alert('Welcome to Svelte!');
	}
</script>

<button onclick={greet}>click me</button>

<style>
	button {
		font-size: 2em;
	}
</style>
```

...into lean, tightly optimized JavaScript.

You can use it to build anything on the web, from standalone components to ambitious full stack apps (using Svelte's companion application framework, [SvelteKit](../kit)) and everything in between.

These pages serve as reference documentation. If you're new to Svelte, we recommend starting with the [interactive tutorial](/tutorial) and coming back here when you have questions.

You can also try Svelte online in the [playground](/playground) or, if you need a more fully-featured environment, on [StackBlitz](https://sveltekit.new).

---
title: Getting started
---

We recommend using [SvelteKit](../kit), which lets you [build almost anything](../kit/project-types). It's the official application framework from the Svelte team and powered by [Vite](https://vite.dev/). Create a new project with:

```sh
npx sv create myapp
cd myapp
npm install
npm run dev
```

Don't worry if you don't know Svelte yet! You can ignore all the nice features SvelteKit brings on top for now and dive into it later.

## Alternatives to SvelteKit

You can also use Svelte directly with Vite via [vite-plugin-svelte](https://github.com/sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte) by running `npm create vite@latest` and selecting the `svelte` option (or, if working with an existing project, adding the plugin to your `vite.config.js` file). With this, `npm run build` will generate HTML, JS, and CSS files inside the `dist` directory. In most cases, you will probably need to [choose a routing library](/packages#routing) as well.

>[!NOTE] Vite is often used in standalone mode to build [single page apps (SPAs)](../kit/glossary#SPA), which you can also [build with SvelteKit](../kit/single-page-apps).

There are also [plugins for other bundlers](/packages#bundler-plugins), but we recommend Vite.

## Editor tooling

The Svelte team maintains a [VS Code extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=svelte.svelte-vscode), and there are integrations with various other [editors](https://sveltesociety.dev/collection/editor-support-c85c080efc292a34) and tools as well.

You can also check your code from the command line using [`npx sv check`](https://svelte.dev/docs/cli/sv-check).


## Getting help

Don't be shy about asking for help in the [Discord chatroom](/chat)! You can also find answers on [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/svelte).

> [!NOTE] **rune** /ruːn/ _noun_
>
> A letter or mark used as a mystical or magic symbol.

Runes are symbols that you use in `.svelte` and `.svelte.js`/`.svelte.ts` files to control the Svelte compiler. If you think of Svelte as a language, runes are part of the syntax — they are _keywords_.

Runes have a `$` prefix and look like functions:

```js
let message = $state('hello');
```

They differ from normal JavaScript functions in important ways, however:

- You don't need to import them — they are part of the language
- They're not values — you can't assign them to a variable or pass them as arguments to a function
- Just like JavaScript keywords, they are only valid in certain positions (the compiler will help you if you put them in the wrong place)

> [!LEGACY]
> Runes didn't exist prior to Svelte 5.

title: $inspect
tags: rune-inspect
---

> [!NOTE] `$inspect` only works during development. In a production build it becomes a noop.

The `$inspect` rune is roughly equivalent to `console.log`, with the exception that it will re-run whenever its argument changes. `$inspect` tracks reactive state deeply, meaning that updating something inside an object or array using fine-grained reactivity will cause it to re-fire:

<!-- codeblock:start {"title":"$inspect(...)"} -->
```svelte
<!--- file: App.svelte --->
<script>
	let count = $state(0);
	let message = $state('hello');

	$inspect(count, message); // will console.log when `count` or `message` change
</script>

<button onclick={() => count++}>Increment</button>
<input bind:value={message} />
```
<!-- codeblock:end -->

On updates, a stack trace will be printed, making it easy to find the origin of a state change (unless you're in the playground, due to technical limitations).

## $inspect(...).with

`$inspect(...)` returns an object with a `with` method, which you can invoke with a callback that will then be invoked instead of `console.log`. The first argument to the callback is either `"init"` or `"update"`; subsequent arguments are the values passed to `$inspect`:

<!-- codeblock:start {"title":"$inspect(...).with(...)"} -->
```svelte
<!--- file: App.svelte --->
<script>
	let count = $state(0);

	$inspect(count).with((type, count) => {
		if (type === 'update') {
			debugger; // or `console.trace`, or whatever you want
		}
	});
</script>

<button onclick={() => count++}>Increment</button>
```
<!-- codeblock:end -->

## $inspect.trace(...)

This rune, added in 5.14, causes the surrounding function to be _traced_ in development. Any time the function re-runs as part of an [effect]($effect) or a [derived]($derived), information will be printed to the console about which pieces of reactive state caused the effect to fire.

```svelte
<script>
	import { doSomeWork } from './elsewhere';

	$effect(() => {
		+++// $inspect.trace must be the first statement of a function body+++
		+++$inspect.trace();+++
		doSomeWork();
	});
</script>
```

`$inspect.trace` takes an optional first argument which will be used as the label.

This ensures you can listen to custom events that have uppercase characters in them. Because events are just attributes, the same rules as for attributes apply: - you can use the shorthand form: `` - you can spread them: `` Timing-wise, event attributes always fire after events from bindings (e.g. `oninput` always fires after an update to `bind:value`). Under the hood, some event handlers are attached directly with `addEventListener`, while others are _delegated_. When using `ontouchstart` and `ontouchmove` event attributes, the handlers are [passive](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventTarget/addEventListener#using_passive_listeners) for better performance. This greatly improves responsiveness by allowing the browser to scroll the document immediately, rather than waiting to see if the event handler calls `event.preventDefault()`. In the very rare cases that you need to prevent these event defaults, you should use [`on`](svelte-events#on) instead (for example inside an action). ### Event delegation To reduce memory footprint and increase performance, Svelte uses a technique called event delegation. This means that for certain events — see the list below — a single event listener at the application root takes responsibility for running any handlers on the event's path. There are a few gotchas to be aware of: - when you manually dispatch an event with a delegated listener, make sure to set the `{ bubbles: true }` option or it won't reach the application root - when using `addEventListener` directly, avoid calling `stopPropagation` or the event won't reach the application root and handlers won't be invoked. report.overview: This is the `sveltejs/svelte` monorepo: a single publishable package (`packages/svelte`, v5.57.1) containing both a compiler that turns `.svelte` components into plain JavaScript modules and a signals-based client/server runtime those modules import at runtime. The compiler runs a strict three-phase pipeline (parse → analyze → transform) with separate client and server code generators, while the runtime implements Svelte 5 runes ($state/$derived/$effect) on top of a push-pull reactive graph with bitflag-tagged signals, batched flushing, and an experimental async/fork mode. It is aimed at framework consumers (SvelteKit, vite-plugin-svelte, svelte-check, the REPL) rather than app authors directly, and is distinctive for shipping unbundled ESM source as the published artifact, generating its error/warning catalogue and its `.d.ts` types from source, and carrying ~3,400 fixture directories as its primary test surface.

system_map.summary: The repo is a pnpm workspace (`pnpm-workspace.yaml` globs `packages/*` and `playgrounds/*`) with exactly one real package, `packages/svelte`, plus a Vite sandbox playground and a Node benchmarking harness at the root. The package has two runtime boundaries encoded in its `exports` map — `browser`/`worker` conditions split every entry into client and server implementations — and a third, the compiler, which is deliberately firewalled from runtime code by a custom ESLint rule. Storage is entirely file-based: there is no database; the only persistent artefacts are compiled test fixtures under `tests/*/samples/*/_output/`, generated docs under `documentation/docs/98-reference/.generated/`, and the checked-in `types/index.d.ts`. External integrations are all build-time libraries (acorn, zimmerframe, esrap, magic-string, devalue) rather than services. Deployment is npm publish via Changesets on push to `main`.

claims.claim: The published artifact is unbundled ESM source: `packages/svelte/package.json` sets `"main"`/`"module"` to `./src/index-client.js` and its `files` array ships `src` directly, so consumers import the raw runtime sources rather than a bundle.

Client/server split is done entirely through export conditions — `.`, `./legacy`, `./reactivity`, and `./store` each map `worker` and `default` to `*-server.js` and `browser` to `*-client.js` (e.g. `./src/index-server.js` vs `./src/index-client.js`).

The compiler's public surface is five functions exported from `src/compiler/index.js`: `compile` (L23), `compileModule` (L69), `parse` (L117), `parseCss` (L131), plus re-exported `preprocess`, `print`, and `migrate` (L202).

Compilation is a fixed three-phase pipeline — `_parse` from `phases/1-parse/index.js`, then `analyze_component` (2-analyze/index.js:333), then `transform_component` (3-transform/index.js) — with `state.reset()` called first to clear module-global compiler state.

Codegen forks per target inside `transform_component`: `options.generate === 'server'` dispatches to `server_component` in `3-transform/server/transform-server.js`, otherwise `client_component` in `3-transform/client/transform-client.js`; both emit an ESTree program that `esrap`'s `print` serialises with a source map.

The runtime reactivity core lives in four files — `internal/client/runtime.js` (866 lines: `get`, `update_reaction`, `update_effect`, `is_dirty`), `reactivity/sources.js`, `reactivity/deriveds.js`, and `reactivity/batch.js` (1475 lines, the `Batch` class and `flushSync`).

Signal identity and lifecycle are encoded as bitflags in `internal/client/constants.js` — `DERIVED`, `EFFECT`, `RENDER_EFFECT`, `BLOCK_EFFECT`, `BRANCH_EFFECT`, `BOUNDARY_EFFECT`, `CLEAN`/`DIRTY`/`MAYBE_DIRTY`, `ASYNC`, `ERROR_VALUE` — rather than as distinct classes.

Server rendering is a string-accumulating `Renderer` class (`internal/server/renderer.js`) with a private `#out` array and a separate `head` sub-renderer; `render()` in `internal/server/index.js:71` is a thin wrapper over `Renderer.render`.

Build commands: `pnpm build` at root fans out to `packages/*`; inside `packages/svelte`, `build` = `rollup -c && pnpm generate && node scripts/check-treeshakeability.js`, where rollup produces only the UMD `compiler/index.js` for CommonJS/browser consumers.

`pnpm generate` is a three-step codegen chain: `scripts/process-messages` (markdown → `errors.js`/`warnings.js` + docs), `scripts/generate-types.js` (dts-buddy), and `scripts/generate-browser-support.ts` (web-features → docs page).

Tests run from the repo root via a single Vitest config that aliases every `svelte/*` import back to `packages/svelte` source using the package's own `exports` map, and picks the `server` export when the importer path contains `_output/server`.

Deployment shape is npm publish driven by Changesets: `.github/workflows/release.yml` runs on push to `main`, calls `changesets/action` with `pnpm changeset:version` / `pnpm changeset:publish`, and sets `NPM_CONFIG_PROVENANCE: true` with `id-token: write`.

The only non-library workspace member is `playgrounds/sandbox`, a Vite + `@sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte` app that consumes `svelte` as `workspace:*` and excludes it from `optimizeDeps` so source edits are picked up without a dev-server restart.

Benchmarking is a separate root-level Node harness (`benchmarking/run.js`) that forks each benchmark into its own child process 'so that heap/GC/JIT state from one benchmark cannot contaminate the others', across compiler, reactivity, and SSR suites.

There is no persistent datastore anywhere in the repo; the closest thing to a storage layer is `compile_directory` in `tests/helpers.js`, which wipes and rewrites `<sample>/_output/{client,server}` on every test run.

feature_catalog.summary: There are no routes or screens — the user-facing surface is a set of npm subpath exports and a compiler API. Broadly: the compiler API (`compile`, `compileModule`, `parse`, `parseCss`, `preprocess`, `print`, `migrate`), the component runtime lifecycle API (`mount`, `hydrate`, `unmount`, `flushSync`, `fork`, `tick`, `untrack`, `settled`), context and lifecycle helpers, and a set of reactive standard-library classes. Around those sit optional subpackages for transitions, animations, easing, motion springs, stores, attachments, and events. Compiler behaviour is configurable through a validated options table, and two experimental features — async mode and `hydratable` — gate themselves on a runtime flag.

claims.claim: `compile(source, options)` returns `{ js, css, warnings, metadata: { runes }, ast }`, where `ast` is post-processed by `to_public_ast` into either a modern AST (metadata stripped via a zimmerframe walk) or a Svelte 4-shaped legacy AST via `convert` from `compiler/legacy.js`.

`parseCss(source)` is a standalone CSS-only entry point that uses `Parser.forCss` — a static factory that `Object.create`s a Parser prototype and skips all Svelte component parsing setup — returning a `StyleSheetFile` node with collected `css_comments`.
`migrate(source, { filename, use_ts })` (2,003 lines in `compiler/migrate/index.js`) is a Svelte 4 → 5 source-to-source codemod exposed publicly through `svelte/compiler`.

`preprocess` accepts a `PreprocessorGroup` or array and applies hooks in a fixed order per preprocessor — `markup`, then `script`, then `style` — matching `<script>`/`<style>` blocks with dedicated regexes and stitching sourcemaps back together.

Compiler options are a declarative validator table in `validate-options.js`: `css` ('injected'|'external'), `cssHash`, `dev`, `discloseVersion`, `hmr`, `modernAst`, `namespace` ('html'|'mathml'|'svg'), `preserveComments`, `preserveWhitespace`, `fragments` ('html'|'tree'), `warningFilter`, and `experimental.async`.

`mount(component, options)` and `hydrate(component, options)` are the two client entry points; both funnel into `_mount`, which accepts `target`, `anchor`, `props`, `events`, `context`, `intro`, and `transformError`.

The top-level `svelte` export surfaces `onMount`, `onDestroy`, `beforeUpdate`, `afterUpdate`, `createEventDispatcher`, `getAbortSignal`, plus re-exports of `flushSync`/`fork`, the context family, `hydratable`, `mount`/`hydrate`/`unmount`, `tick`/`untrack`/`settled`, and `createRawSnippet`.

`getAbortSignal()` lazily creates an `AbortController` on the active reaction (`active_reaction.ac ??= new AbortController()`) and throws `get_abort_signal_outside_reaction` if called outside a derived/effect; the abort reason is the shared `STALE_REACTION` singleton error.
`svelte/reactivity` ships seven reactive primitives: `SvelteDate`, `SvelteSet`, `SvelteMap`, `SvelteURL`, `SvelteURLSearchParams`, `MediaQuery`, and `createSubscriber`.

`svelte/attachments` provides `createAttachmentKey()` (a `Symbol(ATTACHMENT_KEY)` recognised when spread onto an element) and `fromAction()`, which adapts a legacy `use:` action into the newer `{@attach}` form.
`render(component, options)` on the server accepts `props`, `context`, `idPrefix`, `csp`, and `transformError`, and hard-errors with `invalid_csp` if both `csp.hash` and `csp.nonce` are supplied.

`hydratable(key, fn)` is an experimental server→client data-transfer feature: the server side serialises values with `devalue` into a lookup keyed by string, and the client side reads them back out of `window.__svelte.h`; both sides throw `experimental_async_required` when `async_mode_flag` is false.
Legacy Svelte 4 compatibility is a first-class subpackage: `svelte/legacy` exports `createClassComponent`, `asClassComponent`, `run`, and `createBubbler` for imperative/class-component migration.

Dev-mode-only features live under `internal/client/dev/`: `hmr.js` (block-based component hot swap), `ownership.js` (mutation-of-non-bound-prop validation), `inspect.js`, `tracing.js`, `console-log.js`, and `debug.js`.
The sandbox playground offers `pnpm download <url|github-repo|test-name>` and `--create-test`, which drives a headless Chromium via Playwright to pull a reproduction into a local sample directory.

data_flow.summary: There are two distinct data pipelines. The compile-time pipeline moves a `.svelte` string through a hand-written state-machine parser into a Svelte AST, through a zimmerframe scope/analysis walk that attaches `metadata` and binding information, and out through target-specific ESTree builders into code + sourcemap + CSS. The runtime pipeline moves user mutations into `Source` signals, propagates dirtiness lazily through deriveds, collects affected effects into a `Batch`, and flushes them to write DOM. The two never share code — an ESLint rule enforces that runtime files cannot import from `../compiler/` or `#compiler`. State ownership is module-global on both sides: the compiler owns `compiler/state.js`, the runtime owns `active_reaction`/`active_effect`/`current_batch`.

claims.claim: Input boundary for compilation is `remove_bom(source)` followed by `state.reset({ warning, filename })`, which clears `warnings`, `source`, `dev`, `runes`, and installs the user's `warningFilter` — every compile starts from a wiped module-global.

Options arrive from two merged sources: the caller's `CompileOptions` (validated) and `<svelte:options>` attributes parsed out of the source into `parsed.options`, with the in-file values overriding the caller's for `css` and `runes`.

TypeScript is detected before parsing via a `lang=` regex over `<script>` tags in the `Parser` constructor (setting `this.ts`), and TS nodes are then stripped from `fragment`/`instance`/`module` by `remove_typescript_nodes` before analysis ever sees them.

The parser is a mutable state machine: `Parser` holds `index`, `stack`, `fragments`, and loops `state = state(this) || fragment` over `template.length`, with states in `1-parse/state/{fragment,element,tag,text}.js`.

Analysis is a zimmerframe walk over a per-node-type visitor table; the fallthrough `_` visitor reconstructs `svelte-ignore` scope by scanning preceding `Comment` siblings and `leadingComments`, pushing onto `ignore_stack` in `compiler/state.js`.

Scope and binding resolution is separated into `phases/scope.js` (`create_scopes`, `Scope`, `ScopeRoot`, `get_rune`, `set_scope`), and cyclic reactive statements are caught by `utils/check_graph_for_cycles.js`.

CSS flows through its own sub-pipeline inside analysis — `analyze_css`, then `prune` (matching selectors against the template), then `warn_unused` — before `render_stylesheet` emits the final stylesheet in the transform phase.

The output boundary merges sourcemaps twice: `esrap`'s `print` emits a map with `sourceMapContent: source`, then `merge_with_preprocessor_map(js, options, js_source_name)` folds in any preprocessor map supplied via `options.sourcemap`.

On the runtime side, `$state` values pass through `proxy()` in `internal/client/proxy.js`, which refuses non-objects, anything already carrying `STATE_SYMBOL`, anything with `COMPONENT_SYMBOL`, and any object whose prototype is neither `Object.prototype` nor `Array.prototype`.

Dependency tracking is a read-side side effect of `get(signal)`: when `active_reaction` is set and not `untracking`, the signal is appended to `new_deps` (or counted as `skipped_deps` when the read order matches the previous run, avoiding array allocation).

Writes go through `internal_set` in `reactivity/sources.js`, which bumps the global `write_version` (via `increment_write_version` in runtime.js) and schedules dependents; `old_values` is a module-level `Map` used to restore pre-batch values.

Effects are not run on write — they are collected into the singleton `current_batch` (`Batch.ensure()`), which owns `schedule`, `capture`, `apply`, `flush`, `discard`, and `settled`, and clears `collected_effects`/`legacy_updates`/`old_values` in its `finally` block.

Server output is accumulated as an array of strings and nested `Renderer` children in `#out`, with `head()` creating a second Renderer tagged `type = 'head'` so head content can be emitted out of document order.
Escaping is centralised in the standalone `src/escaping.js`: `escape_html(value, is_attr)` uses `/[&"<]/g` for attributes and `/[&<]/g` for content, escaping only `&`, `"`, and `<`.

Compile-time and runtime data are kept structurally disjoint by a bespoke ESLint rule `no_compiler_imports`, which string-searches every file under `src/` (excluding `src/compiler/`) for `../compiler/` or `#compiler` and reports a hard error.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows dominate. (1) Compile: `compile()` resets global state, validates options, parses, strips TS, analyzes, transforms, and re-attaches a public AST. (2) Client startup: `mount()` initialises DOM operation caches, opens a root effect and an error boundary, pushes a component context, invokes the compiled component function, and returns its exports. (3) Update: a `$state` write sets a source, which schedules its reactions into a `Batch`, which is flushed on the microtask or synchronously via `flushSync`. A fourth, the SSR→hydrate round trip, is what the test harness itself exercises on every fixture.

claims.claim: Compile trace: `remove_bom` → `state.reset` → `validate_component_options` → `_parse(source)` → destructure `parsed.options` into `combined_options` → conditional `remove_typescript_nodes` → `analyze_component(parsed, source, combined_options)` → `transform_component(analysis, source, combined_options)` → `to_public_ast`.

Transform trace (client): `client_component` seeds state with `hoisted: [b.import_all('$', 'svelte/internal/client')]` and an empty `templates` Map, walks the template AST with the visitor table, appends `template.body` into `component_block.body`, pushes a `$$css` const when styles are injected, then re-orders `module.body` so imports stay on top followed by hoisted statements.

Mount trace: `mount()` → `_mount()` → `init_operations()` → `component_root(...)` → create an anchor text node via `target.appendChild(create_text())` → `boundary(anchor, { pending }, cb)` → `push({})` to open a component context → assign `props.$$events` if `events` given → set `should_intro = intro` → call `Component(anchor_node, props)`.

Hydrate trace: `hydrate()` forces `intro ?? false`, scans forward from `get_first_child(target)` for a comment node whose `data === HYDRATION_START`, throws `HYDRATION_ERROR` if absent, calls `set_hydrating(true)` + `set_hydrate_node(anchor)`, then delegates to the same `_mount` with the discovered anchor.

Hydration failure recovery: non-Svelte errors are `console.warn`ed, `options.recover === false` escalates to `e.hydration_failed()`, otherwise `init_operations()` + `clear_text_content(target)` runs and the component falls back to a fresh `mount(component, options)` — with `hydrating`/`hydrate_node` restored in `finally`.

Read trace: `get(signal)` adds the signal to `captured_signals`, registers the dependency on `active_reaction`, and takes one of two registration paths depending on whether `REACTION_IS_UPDATING` is set — the post-`await` path deduplicates with `includes.call` because `remove_reactions` would otherwise disconnect still-live deps.

Synchronous flush trace: `flushSync(fn)` sets `is_flushing_sync`, flushes any non-fork `current_batch` before running `fn`, then loops `flush_tasks()` + `current_batch.flush()` until `current_batch === null`, restoring the previous flag in `finally`.

Batch flush trace: `Batch.flush()` clears DEV `source_stacks`, sets `is_processing = true` and `current_batch = this`, runs the private `#process()`, then in `finally` resets `flush_count`, `last_scheduled_effect`, `collected_effects`, `legacy_updates`, `current_batch`, `batch_values`, and `old_values`.

`{@html}` trace: the `html()` block runs inside a `template_effect`, short-circuits on unchanged value, uses `parent_node.innerHTML = value` when it is the only child, otherwise builds a `<template>`/`<svg>`/`<math>` wrapper, sets `wrapper.innerHTML`, and inserts the resulting nodes via `anchor.before(...)`.

HMR trace: `hmr(fn)` wraps the component in a `source(fn)` signal; a `block()` effect reads it, and on change deletes every key from the old `instance`, calls `destroy_effect(effect)`, and re-creates a `branch()` with `set_should_intro(false)` so the swap plays no transitions.

Test trace: `runtime_suite` → `common_setup` builds a `CompileOptions` (forcing `accessors: true` by default and `experimental.async` from `runes && async_mode`) and calls `compile_directory(cwd, 'client')` and `compile_directory(cwd, 'server')` → `run_test_variant` imports from `_output/` and calls `render`, `mount`, or `hydrate` per variant.

`compile_directory` trace: wipe `_output/<generate>`, glob every non-`_`-prefixed file, route `.svelte.js` through `compileModule`, plain `.js` through a re-export shim so `_config.js` can share module state, and `.svelte` through optional `preprocess` then `compile`, honouring `.client.svelte`/`.server.svelte` suffixes.

Message codegen trace: `scripts/process-messages/index.js` deletes and recreates `documentation/docs/98-reference/.generated`, walks `messages/<category>/*.md`, matches `## CODE` headings, and throws on any duplicate code across categories.

Benchmark trace: `benchmarking/run.js` in parent mode filters suites by `process.argv` substrings and forks one child per benchmark; in child mode (`BENCH_SINGLE` set) it calls `$.push({}, true)`, runs the benchmark under `with_cpu_profile`, `$.pop()`s, and `process.send`s the result with an exit callback.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is Vitest-driven with a fixture-directory convention: 22 suites under `packages/svelte/tests/`, each a `test.ts` plus a `samples/` directory where every subdirectory is one test, optionally configured by a `_config.js`. Coverage is enormous by fixture count — 1,209 legacy runtime samples, 1,054 runes runtime samples, 335 validator samples, 184 CSS samples — and the runtime suites multiply each by four variants (dom, hydrate, ssr, async-ssr). Real-browser coverage is narrow: only `runtime-browser` (35 samples) and the custom-elements samples run under Playwright Chromium. CI runs the full suite on Node 20/22/24 across Windows, macOS, and Ubuntu, plus a no-async pass, a tsgo typecheck, a lint/types-drift gate, and a benchmark job.

claims.claim: Vitest 4 is the single test runner, configured once at the repo root with `include` patterns `packages/svelte/**/*.test.ts`, `packages/svelte/tests/*/test.ts`, and `packages/svelte/tests/runtime-browser/test-ssr.ts`, and `**/samples/**` excluded so fixtures are never collected as tests.

The global `testTimeout` is raised to 30s with an in-file rationale: dev-mode tests that trip `effect_update_depth_exceeded` allocate ~1000 Error objects per flush for stack tracking, which overruns the 5s default under Vitest 4.

`tests/suite.ts` provides the two harness primitives: `suite()` (one `it` per sample dir) and `suite_with_variants()` (one `it` per dir × variant, with a `should_skip_variant` hook returning `true` to skip or `'no-test'` to omit entirely).

Test selection supports both `pnpm test <suite> -t <name>` and a `FILTER` env var that compiles to an anchored or `/regex/` RegExp in `suite.ts`, plus per-config `skip`/`solo`/`timeout` flags on `BaseTest`.
Runtime suites run four variants per sample — `dom`, `hydrate`, `ssr`, `async-ssr` — with `async-ssr` gated on both runes mode and `async_mode` (i.e. `process.env.SVELTE_NO_ASYNC !== 'true'`).

Fixture counts skew heavily toward runtime behaviour: `runtime-legacy/samples` (1209), `runtime-runes/samples` (1054), `validator/samples` (335), `css/samples` (184), `compiler-errors/samples` (146), `server-side-rendering/samples` (132).

Real-browser testing is limited to `tests/runtime-browser/test.ts`, which launches a single Chromium via `@playwright/test`, bundles each sample with `esbuild`, and runs `dom`/`hydrate` variants plus a separate `custom-elements-samples` suite — with `retry: 1` on CI because 'browser tests are brittle and slow on CI'.

XHTML/XML-document behaviour gets its own environment: `vitest-xhtml-environment.ts` wraps the jsdom builtin with `contentType: 'application/xhtml+xml'`, consumed by `tests/runtime-xhtml/test.ts` via a `@vitest-environment` pragma (13 samples).

Unit tests colocated with source are rare — only `src/utils.test.ts`, `src/internal/client/proxy.test.ts`, `src/internal/client/error-handling.test.ts`, the four `src/reactivity/*.test.ts` files, and `src/internal/server/{crypto,hydratable,renderer}.test.ts`.

Snapshot-style suites (`snapshot`, `parser-modern`, `parser-legacy`, `print`, `sourcemaps`) assert generated output against checked-in expectations and are regenerated with `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=true pnpm test`.

CI's `Tests` job matrixes Node 20 across windows/macOS/ubuntu plus Node 22 and 24 on ubuntu, installs only Chromium (`PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD: '1'` then `pnpm playwright install chromium`), with a 15-minute timeout.
A dedicated `TestNoAsync` job re-runs only `runtime-runes` with `SVELTE_NO_ASYNC: true`, guarding the non-async code path that the default run never exercises.

The `Lint` job doubles as a drift gate: after `pnpm build` it fails if `git status --porcelain` is non-empty (generated types out of date) and separately checks `documentation/docs/07-misc/.generated/` for a stale browser-support page.
Coverage is configured (v8 provider, `lcov` + `html`, scoped to `packages/svelte/src/**`, `reportOnFailure: true`) but no CI job invokes it or enforces a threshold.
`tests/manual/` exists as a suite directory with no `test.ts` and no samples, so nothing in it runs under `pnpm test`.

risk_map.summary: The highest-severity surfaces are the two `innerHTML` sinks (`{@html}` and the template reconciler) and the server-side CSP/hash path, all of which are correct-by-design but unforgiving of misuse. Structurally, the biggest fragility is module-global mutable state on both sides of the codebase — `compiler/state.js` makes `compile()` non-reentrant, and `active_reaction`/`active_effect`/`current_batch`/`old_values` make the runtime a single-threaded global machine where any missed `finally` leaks state across components. Blast radius is concentrated in `runtime.js`, `reactivity/batch.js`, and `phases/2-analyze/index.js`, each of which sits under thousands of fixtures. Legacy code is not dead but is a permanent second code path: legacy mode, legacy AST conversion, and `beforeUpdate`/`afterUpdate` all have their own branches.

claims.claim: `{@html}` is the primary XSS surface and is documented as such: `html()` assigns user values straight to `parent_node.innerHTML` or `wrapper.innerHTML` with no sanitisation, relying only on the fact that `innerHTML` does not execute `<script>`.

A second `innerHTML` sink exists in the template reconciler, where compiled template strings are assigned via `create_trusted_html(html.replaceAll('<!>', '<!---->'))` — safe only because the input is compiler-generated rather than user-supplied.

`escape_html` escapes only `&`, `<`, and (in attribute mode) `"` — single quotes and `>` are deliberately not escaped, so any compiler codegen path that emits a single-quoted attribute without also escaping would be an injection hole.

The server-side CSP path computes `sha256` hashes over inline script bodies and pushes them onto `global.csp.script_hashes`; `invalid_csp` is thrown only for the hash+nonce combination, and the nonce is interpolated into the attribute unescaped (` nonce="${this.global.csp.nonce}"`).

`internal/server/crypto.js` performs a deliberately obfuscated dynamic import — `import(/* @vite-ignore */ module_name)` on the string `'node:crypto'` — specifically so static analysers cannot see the Node dependency; this defeats bundler and supply-chain tooling that relies on static import graphs.

The compiler is not reentrant: `compiler/state.js` holds `warnings`, `source`, `filename`, `dev`, `runes`, `ignore_stack`, and `ignore_map` as module-level `let`s that `reset()` clobbers, so two concurrent `compile()` calls in one process would interleave diagnostics.

The runtime has the same shape of risk at larger scale: `active_reaction`, `active_effect`, `untracking`, `new_deps`, `skipped_deps`, `untracked_writes`, `write_version`, and `update_version` are all module-level mutable globals in `runtime.js`.

`Batch.flush()` relies entirely on its `finally` block to reset seven pieces of cross-cutting state (`flush_count`, `last_scheduled_effect`, `collected_effects`, `legacy_updates`, `current_batch`, `batch_values`, `old_values`); an early return added above that block would leave the whole runtime wedged.

Signal semantics are encoded in 26 overlapping bitflags, and two of them collide by design — `MANAGED_EFFECT` and `DESTROYING` both use `1 << 24`, and `EFFECT_OFFSCREEN` and `DESTROYING` both use `1 << 25` — meaning correctness depends on flags never co-occurring on the same signal.

Hydration failure is silently recoverable by default: any non-Svelte error triggers `console.warn` + full client re-render, so a genuine SSR/CSR divergence only surfaces as a warning unless the consumer passes `recover: false`.

Legacy Svelte 4 support is a permanently parallel code path, not dead code: `legacy_mode_flag`, `compiler/legacy.js`'s AST `convert`, `legacy_pre_effect`/`legacy_pre_effect_reset`, `internal/client/dev/legacy.js`, and the `beforeUpdate`/`afterUpdate` callback queue all exist solely for it.

Async mode is experimental and dual-pathed — `enable_async_mode_flag` is set only by importing `svelte/internal/flags/async`, and there is a `disable_async_mode_flag` explicitly annotated 'ONLY USE THIS DURING TESTING' — so the non-async path is only covered by the single `TestNoAsync` CI job.

The `autofix.yml` workflow runs on `issue_comment` with `contents: write` and pushes a commit to the PR head branch; it mitigates the obvious fork risk by refusing non-same-repo PRs and gating on `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR` author association.

`ecosystem-ci-trigger.yml` mints a GitHub App token from `ECOSYSTEM_CI_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` and includes an explicit TOCTOU guard: it fails with a 'Security warning' if `pr.head.repo.pushed_at` is newer than the triggering comment's `created_at`.

Four ESLint rules are disabled repo-wide with a `TODO: enable these rules` comment — `@stylistic/quotes`, `@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars`, and `prefer-const` — so unused variables and accidental `let` are currently unenforced across all of `src/`.

`playgrounds/sandbox/scripts/download.js` combines `execSync` from `node:child_process`, `new URL(url_arg)` on user input, and a Playwright Chromium launch against arbitrary URLs — the only shell-out + arbitrary-network path in the repo, and it is unlinted (`playgrounds/sandbox/**` is in the ESLint ignore list).

extension_points.summary: Almost every extension point is a plain object literal keyed by node type or property name, which makes adding language features mechanical: drop a file into the right `visitors/` directory and register it in the table. The three big ones are the analysis visitor table, the client and server transform visitor tables, and the `binding_properties` registry that defines what `bind:` can target. Below those sit the compiler options validator table, the markdown-driven message catalogue, the preprocessor hook interface, and the export map itself. On the runtime side, `createSubscriber` and `createAttachmentKey` are the sanctioned APIs for library authors who need to plug into reactivity and element lifecycle without touching internals.

claims.claim: Adding a new analysable node type means creating `phases/2-analyze/visitors/<NodeType>.js` and adding it to the `visitors` object in `2-analyze/index.js` — the file currently imports ~60 such visitors explicitly by name.

Client codegen has a parallel registry: `const visitors = {...}` at `3-transform/client/transform-client.js:65`, backed by ~45 files in `3-transform/client/visitors/` plus a `shared/` directory for logic common to both targets.

The server codegen mirrors it in `3-transform/server/transform-server.js` exporting `server_component` and `server_module`, so a new template feature generally requires a matching visitor in both client and server visitor directories.

`phases/bindings.js` exports `binding_properties`, a ~47-entry `Record<string, BindingProperty>` where each entry declares `event`, `bidirectional`, `omit_in_ssr`, `valid_elements`, and `invalid_elements` — this is the single table that defines which `bind:` directives exist.

New compiler options are registered declaratively in `validate-options.js` using the `string()`, `boolean()`, `list()`, `fun()`, and `warning()` combinators, split between `common_options` and `component_options`.

New errors/warnings are added as markdown `## CODE` sections under `packages/svelte/messages/<category>/*.md` across eight categories (client/server/shared/compile × errors/warnings); `scripts/process-messages` generates both the runtime throwers and the reference docs from them.

The generated message modules are explicitly excluded from linting (`src/compiler/errors.js`, `src/internal/client/errors.js`, `src/internal/client/warnings.js`, `src/internal/shared/warnings.js`, `src/internal/server/warnings.js`), which is the signal that they must never be hand-edited.

The public plugin interface for build tooling is `PreprocessorGroup` — an object with optional `markup`, `script`, and `style` async hooks, each receiving `{ content, attributes, markup, filename }` and returning `{ code, map }`.

New public subpaths are added by editing the `exports` map in `packages/svelte/package.json`; `scripts/check-treeshakeability.js` then reads that same map to resolve each entry and asserts via a rollup bundle that importing it produces no side effects.

`createSubscriber` (in `src/reactivity/create-subscriber.js`, exported from `svelte/reactivity`) is the sanctioned hook for library authors wiring external event sources into Svelte's reactivity — it is how `MediaQuery` is built.

`createAttachmentKey()` is the programmatic extension point for element lifecycle: it returns a `Symbol(ATTACHMENT_KEY)` that the runtime recognises when spread onto an element, letting library authors attach behaviour without a `use:` directive.

New block types plug into `internal/client/dom/blocks/` — the directory currently holds `async`, `await`, `boundary`, `branches`, `css-props`, `each`, `html`, `if`, `key`, `slot`, `snippet`, `svelte-component`, `svelte-element`, and `svelte-head`, each a function invoked by generated code.

New effect kinds are created through the factory family in `reactivity/effects.js` — `user_effect`, `user_pre_effect`, `eager_effect`, `effect_root`, `component_root`, `render_effect`, `template_effect`, `block`, `managed`, `branch`, `async_effect` — all of which funnel into a shared internal `create_effect` with different flag combinations.
Agent-facing workflows are themselves extensible via `.agents/skills/`, which currently holds one skill (`performance-investigation`) that `AGENTS.md` routes to by name.

agent_handoff.summary: Read `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` first — the repo's own agent guide makes the PR template mandatory and forbids submitting without a full test run. The dominant convention is `snake_case` internally, `camelCase` publicly; the dominant workflow is add a fixture directory, not a new test file. The two hard edit boundaries are generated files (types, error/warning modules, generated docs) and the compiler/runtime import firewall. Expect long feedback loops: the full suite covers ~3,400 fixtures across 4 variants, so filter aggressively while iterating and only run the full suite before opening a PR.

claims.claim: `AGENTS.md` is explicit that `CONTRIBUTING.md` must also be read, that `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` must be read and filled out correctly for any PR, and that PRs must not be submitted without running the full test suite.

Naming convention is enforced, not advisory: `snake_case` for internal variables and methods, `camelCase` for public ones, backed by the `lube/svelte-naming-convention` ESLint rule set to `error` with `fixSameNames: true`.

Never hand-edit `packages/svelte/types/index.d.ts`, `src/compiler/errors.js`, or the four `warnings.js` modules — they are generated by `pnpm generate` and CI fails the `Lint` job if `git status` is dirty after `pnpm build`.

Never import from `../compiler/` or `#compiler` inside `packages/svelte/src/**` outside `src/compiler/**` — the custom `no_compiler_imports` rule string-searches the file text and rejects even JSDoc type references.

Adding a test means creating a directory under `packages/svelte/tests/<suite>/samples/`, optionally with a `_config.js` default-exporting the config object — `for_each_dir` in `suite.ts` discovers it automatically, so no test file is edited.
Files prefixed with `_` inside a sample directory are excluded from compilation by `compile_directory`, which is how `_config.js` coexists with the component files it tests.
A sample directory containing only `_output` or `_actual.json` is treated as leftover from another branch and silently skipped — so a suite that appears to pass may simply not have run.
Tests require Chromium to be installed first (`pnpm playwright install chromium`) or the `runtime-browser` and custom-elements suites will fail to launch.
Iterate with `pnpm test <suite>`, `pnpm test <suite> -t <name>`, or `FILTER=<name> pnpm test <suite>`; snapshot suites are regenerated with `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=true pnpm test`.

Typechecking is a three-project run inside `packages/svelte`: `tsc --project tsconfig.runtime.json && tsc && cd ./tests/types && tsc` — the `tests/types` project exists purely to typecheck public API ergonomics (`actions.ts`, `snippet.ts`, `store.ts`, `bindings.svelte`, …).

Any change under `packages/svelte/src` requires a changeset (`npx changeset`) per the PR template; the root `changeset:version` script also runs `pnpm -r generate:version` so `src/version.js` stays in sync.

For performance work, use the `performance-investigation` skill: run `pnpm bench:compare main <branch>`, read `benchmarking/compare/.results/report.txt`, then diff the per-benchmark `.md` CPU-profile summaries, and re-run `pnpm test runtime-runes` afterward.
Files to read first for the compiler: `src/compiler/index.js`, `phases/1-parse/index.js`, `phases/2-analyze/index.js`, `phases/3-transform/index.js`, `phases/scope.js`, `phases/bindings.js`.

Files to read first for the runtime: `internal/client/constants.js` (the flag vocabulary, which nothing else makes sense without), `internal/client/runtime.js`, `reactivity/{sources,deriveds,effects,batch}.js`, `internal/client/render.js`, `internal/client/proxy.js`.

Known trap: `tests/README.md` is a stale migration-era document listing 'TODOs' and 'tests not copied over yet' from the Svelte 4→5 rewrite; treat it as historical context rather than current guidance.

Known trap: `pnpm-workspace.yaml` sets `minimumReleaseAge: 2880` and `blockExoticSubdeps: true`, so adding a freshly-published third-party dependency will be rejected unless it is on the `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` list.

SHAPE. A pnpm workspace with one real package, `packages/svelte`, plus `playgrounds/sandbox` (a Vite demo app) and root-level `benchmarking/` and `documentation/`. The package is published as unbundled ESM source: `package.json` points `main`/`module` at `./src/index-client.js` and ships `src/` directly. The only bundled output is the UMD `compiler/index.js` produced by `rollup.config.js`.

TWO HALVES. (1) The compiler in `src/compiler/`: `compile()` in `index.js` runs `state.reset()` → `validate_component_options` → `_parse` (a hand-written state machine in `phases/1-parse/`) → optional `remove_typescript_nodes` → `analyze_component` (`phases/2-analyze/index.js`, a zimmerframe walk over a ~60-entry visitor table) → `transform_component` (`phases/3-transform/index.js`, which forks to `client_component` or `server_component` and serialises via `esrap`). (2) The runtime in `src/internal/`: a signals graph where every value carries bitflags from `internal/client/constants.js` (`DERIVED`, `EFFECT`, `BLOCK_EFFECT`, `CLEAN`/`DIRTY`/`MAYBE_DIRTY`, `ASYNC`). Reads register deps in `get()` (`runtime.js`), writes go through `internal_set` (`reactivity/sources.js`), and effects are collected into a `Batch` (`reactivity/batch.js`) flushed on a microtask or by `flushSync`. `mount`/`hydrate`/`unmount` live in `internal/client/render.js`; SSR is a string-accumulating `Renderer` in `internal/server/renderer.js`.

HARD BOUNDARIES. Runtime code may not import from `../compiler/` or `#compiler` — a custom ESLint rule (`no_compiler_imports` in `eslint.config.js`) string-searches file text and rejects even JSDoc references. Never hand-edit generated files: `types/index.d.ts`, `src/compiler/errors.js`, and the `warnings.js` modules all come from `pnpm generate`, and CI fails if `git status` is dirty after `pnpm build`. Errors and warnings are authored as `## CODE` markdown sections under `packages/svelte/messages/`.

TESTING. Vitest, configured once at the repo root. 22 suites under `packages/svelte/tests/`, each a `test.ts` plus a `samples/` directory where every subdirectory is one test, optionally configured by a `_config.js` (files prefixed `_` are not compiled). Runtime suites run four variants per sample: `dom`, `hydrate`, `ssr`, `async-ssr`. Install Chromium first (`pnpm playwright install chromium`). Iterate with `pnpm test <suite> -t <name>` or `FILTER=<name> pnpm test <suite>`; regenerate snapshots with `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=true pnpm test`. Typecheck with `pnpm check` inside `packages/svelte`; lint with `pnpm lint`.

CONVENTIONS. `snake_case` internally, `camelCase` publicly (enforced by `lube/svelte-naming-convention`). Any change under `packages/svelte/src` needs a changeset. Prefix PR titles with `feat:`/`fix:`/`chore:`/`docs:`.

WATCH OUT FOR. Module-global mutable state on both sides — `compiler/state.js` makes `compile()` non-reentrant, and `runtime.js` keeps `active_reaction`/`active_effect`/`current_batch` as globals whose reset depends on `finally` blocks. `{@html}` (`dom/blocks/html.js`) and the reconciler are raw `innerHTML` sinks. Async mode is experimental and gated on `async_mode_flag`; the non-async path is only covered by the `TestNoAsync` CI job. Legacy Svelte 4 support is a permanent parallel code path, not dead code. `tests/README.md` is a stale migration-era document — don't trust it.
